doc.title: John Beal interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 18, 2024

chapter: Studio work and learning the craft
title: Dixieland gig, Bucky Pizzarelli and Stokowski
summary: Beal tells of a fun Dixieland gig, his friendship with Bucky Pizzarelli and Ruby Braff albums, and playing principal bass for Stokowski.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I once asked Bucky Pizzarelli what kind of date might he have done that would be worth coming home and talking to his wife Ruth about — “Hey guess what occurred today.” Do you have one of those, like with all the work you do, what is worth bringing up when you get home?

Oh I always comment about what I just did. You know like I played a Dixieland gig Sunday night and I came home and told my wife, “That was like a lot of fun, like I really loved playing that bass. I got the sound that I wanted to get, you know, you don’t play with any microphone or amplifier and the place was sold out to a tour of Japanese tourists, older people. And they ended up like really getting into this, dancing and throwing up their hands and during the break they’d run up on the bandstand and pose

with pictures, you know put their arms around you. It was really a lot of fun you know. So I just describe that. And I describe my impressions of different jobs. Bucky, Bucky was a great friend of mine from way back and I loved playing with him. In fact we played on a Ruby Braff album, a couple of them. And you know we were just compatible.
That’s an interesting concept about — I used to think that almost all veteran jazz people all got along.
Yeah. You think that’s true then?

I agree, yeah. We’re all in the same love situation, you know? We like music. We like jazz. I mean jazz has been my first preference. But I like playing symphonic stuff. I played with Leopold Stokowski and that was a lot of fun. In his last three years in this country, and I was fortunate enough to get principal bass in his orchestra and you’d always end up sweating with him you know, even if you were hung over, you’d go into a rehearsal and in about a half hour you’re sweating you know. He really made you play.
